catalog_citation: Cushing, J. N. (1871). Grammar of the Shan Language. Rangoon: American Mission Press. (archive.org item grammar_of_the_shan_language, Google Books scan, djvu text)
catalog_locator: Chapter III 'The Tones of the Shan Language', sections 32-35 (pp. 8-9)
catalog_quote: 32. The Shan is a tonal language. Accuracy in speaking it depends upon an exact knowledge of the tones and the power of enunciating them. A single combination may have a variety of distinct meanings, according to the accent of the voice with which it is uttered. 33. The precise extent and limitations of the tones can only be learned from the lips of a native teacher ... 34. Some combinations admit of only one tone, a short abrupt sound, which is the same as the fifth tone mentioned in § 35. ... 35. For other combinations, five tones may be readily distinguished, though only three of them are generally given by natives in reciting the Primer. The first is the natural pitch of the voice with a rising inflection at the end, and may be called the natural tone. The second is a deep bass tone, and may be called the grave tone. The third is the straightforward tone. The fourth is the high tone…

Deciding source Lengtai 2009 sec. 3.1.2 pp. 26-30 + sec. 5.1.1 p. 95; Cushing 1871 pp. 8-9 and Soh 2019 pp. 27-30 kept as tone confirmations. Same coding the catalog already gives Pa-O (paok1235, Thanamteun 2000 Mahidol MA, identical 'strong stress on the final syllable of the phonological word' framework -> fixed-unreviewed final stress) and, mutatis mutandis, Thai (fixed-dominant, final).

sources.citation: Cushing, J. N. 1888. Elementary Handbook of the Shan Language. Rangoon: American Baptist Mission Press. (archive.org item elementary-handbook-of-the-shan-language, djvu text)
sources.quote: 'Like the other languages of Farther India, it is tonal. No one can speak it accurately without mastering the tones. ... There are five tones which have been described in the Grammar section 32. Of these tones there are three series, viz. closed, mediate, and open.' No stress/accent statement (a full-text search for stress/accent full text).

sources.citation: Soh, Jyr Minn. 2019. Serial verb constructions in Tai Long Shan. MA thesis, Nanyang Technological University (supervisors A. Coupe, R. LaPolla). 171 pp. hdl.handle.net/10356/106030
sources.quote: p. 27: 'Shan is traditionally identified as a monosyllabic language, but compounding is also a part of their word formation ... The canonical TLS syllable consists of an obligatory vowel and tone. ... (C1)(G1)V1(V2)(C2)T'. p. 30: 'TLS has five distinct tones: low slightly falling then rising /214/, low slightly falling /21/, high slightly falling /43/, high level /44/, and high falling /52/. Unchecked syllables of TLS have all five tonal contrasts while checked syllables have four tonal contrasts.' No mention of stress anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/prosod/unstressed/iambic/sesquisyllabi
